drug_class: Monoclonal antibody / EGFR inhibitor (targeted cancer therapy)
purpose: Panitumumab is used to treat a specific type of colorectal cancer (cancer of the colon or rectum) that has spread to other parts of the body. It is typically used when other chemotherapy treatments have not worked or have stopped working. Your doctor will test your tumor to make sure this medicine is right for your type of cancer.
how_it_works: Cancer cells sometimes have a protein on their surface called EGFR (epidermal growth factor receptor) that helps them grow and multiply out of control. Panitumumab works like a targeted 'guided missile' — it attaches to that EGFR protein and blocks it, which slows down or stops the cancer cells from growing. Because it targets a specific protein, it works differently from traditional chemotherapy.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects involve the skin — you may notice a rash (often on the face, chest, or back), dry or cracked skin, itching, or nail changes. Other common side effects include low magnesium levels in your blood (which can cause muscle cramps or fatigue), diarrhea, mouth sores, nausea, and tiredness. Skin reactions are very common with this medication — your care team will help you manage them.
warnings: A serious skin rash can develop and in rare cases can become severe or get infected — let your doctor know right away if your skin gets very painful, blistered, or infected. This medication can cause dangerously low levels of magnesium and other electrolytes in your blood, so your doctor will check your blood regularly. Panitumumab can cause serious lung problems (inflammation in the lungs) — tell your doctor immediately if you develop new or worsening shortness of breath or cough. It can also cause eye irritation and dryness. This drug should NOT be used if your tumor has a mutation in the RAS gene, as it will not work and may cause harm. Do not use if you are pregnant or breastfeeding.
typical_dosing: Panitumumab is given as an IV infusion (a drip directly into a vein) by a healthcare provider in a clinic or infusion center — you cannot take it at home as a pill. The typical dose is 6 mg per kilogram of your body weight, given once every 2 weeks. Each infusion usually takes about 60 minutes. Your doctor may adjust your dose depending on how you tolerate the medication.
